sections.title: Purification in Water
sections.html:
It is a Torah mitzva that all matters of sanctity in the Temple service, as well as touching the meat of the sacrifices, ḥalla, and the produce of teruma and ma'aser sheni, and eating them, be carried out by people who are tahor (ritually pure). As we learned (above 1:2), tum'a (ritual impurity) is connected to death; therefore the most severe tum'a is that of a corpse, which is called 'avi avot ha-tum'a' (the ultimate source of impurity). A less severe tum'a is the tum'a caused by discharges that could have brought life and were lost, such as the tum'a of nidda (a menstruant woman) and of semen, or by discharges that reflect damage to the life-bringing system, such as the tum'a of a zav and a zava. The order of the purification process corresponds to the severity of the tum'a: one who became tamei through a corpse must wait seven days; on the third and the seventh day, water containing the ashes of the red heifer must be sprinkled upon him, and on the seventh day he immerses, and at its end he becomes tahor. A zav and a zava must wait seven clean days (shiv'a neki'im) and immerse, without any need for sprinkling of the red heifer's ash water. A man or a woman who became tamei through semen, as well as those who touch the carcass of a domestic or wild animal or a creeping creature (sheretz), are tamei until the end of the day and become tahor through immersion. The laws of purity are very numerous, and an entire order out of the six orders of the Mishna is devoted to them; however, one rule applies to all who are tamei: their purification is not complete without tevila (immersion) in water.

As for the reason for the mitzva to become purified in water, one may say that water preceded the appearance of life, as it is stated (Bereishit 1:1-2): "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. And the earth was unformed and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the water." On the first day God created light, in order to give direction to the world through it, and the world was still full of water and surrounded by it. On the second day (ibid. 6-7): "And God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide between water and water. And God made the firmament, and divided between the water which was under the firmament and the water which was above the firmament, and it was so." And the entire earth was still flooded with water. On the third day: "And God said: Let the water under the heavens be gathered together to one place, and let the dry land appear, and it was so. And God called the dry land earth, and the gathering of the water He called seas, and God saw that it was good" (ibid. 9-10). Thus water is the foundation from which life in the world began, and one who is tamei, who has become distanced from the root of life, goes back and immerses entirely in water, and thereby returns to the root of his vitality, and is as if created anew, and becomes tahor (more on this above 1:11-12).

After the Temple was destroyed and Israel was exiled from its land, purity ceased from Israel; yet an important and sanctified purity still remained for us, namely purification from the tum'a of nidda, because the tum'a of nidda concerns not only entering the Temple and eating sacred foods, but also the closeness between husband and wife. Indeed, in the sanctified bond between a man and his wife the essence of purity and holiness in Israel has remained, as Rabbi Akiva said of a man and a woman who merit to live in faithfulness, that the Shekhina dwells between them (Sota 17a), for the root of the love, life and unity between a man and his wife is in the Holy of Holies (above 1:9-10; Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 1:5-7).

Because of the great stature of the holiness of Israel, and because the mikva (ritual bath) is used regularly by a large public of women, the custom of Israel is to be meticulous lekhatḥila (from the outset) in the laws of the mikva, and when possible, they are stringent to build it in a way that will be kosher even according to individual opinions that were not accepted as halakha (Tashbetz 1:17; Da'at Kohen 116). However, when the stringency would make it difficult to establish a mikva, one should not be stringent. All the more so, one should not be stringent with new stringencies, which would cast aspersions on the women who immersed in the past (Maharik 56; Da'at Kohen 117; 125).

Because of the great importance of the mikva, every community is obligated to build a mikva (Rema, ḤM 163:3). Likewise, it is a mitzva to build a mikva that is as beautiful, clean and pleasant as possible (Ḥiddushei Rabbi Akiva Eiger 39).

sections.title: Pure Water in the Ground
sections.html:
A person's purification from his tum'a is accomplished by immersing the entire body at once in pure water that is gathered in the ground, that is, in groundwater that issued from a spring, or in rainwater that collected in the ground. For as long as this water is in the ground in its natural way, it is pure and cannot become tamei, as it is stated (Vayikra 11:36): "Only a spring or a cistern, a gathering of water, shall be pure." But water that was detached from the ground by a person or by vessels can become tamei, and consequently, when someone who is tamei touches it, the water becomes tamei and can no longer purify him (Ḥatam Sofer, YD 213).

Any place in the ground in which water can gather is fit for a mikva, including a spring, a sea, and a pit hewn in the ground. A pool built of bricks and concrete inside a building or on its roof, even atop a hundred stories, is also fit for a mikva. For since the building is attached to the ground in the manner of a building, the pool built above it is also considered attached to the ground. But water collected inside a vessel, even if the vessel is huge, such as a plastic pool or a ship, can become tamei, since it is not gathered in a place that is attached to the ground, and it is consequently unfit for a mikva.

One who wishes to make a mikva by means of a large vessel, such as a plastic or metal tank, must first nullify its status as a vessel by piercing a hole in its bottom with a diameter of about eight cm. In addition, he must attach the pierced vessel to the ground with concrete or the like, or by placing it in a deep excavation in the ground. After the pierced vessel is attached to the ground, the hole is sealed by the ground, and one may additionally seal it with any material (Rambam; SA 201:7).

When building a mikva, one may use iron rods to reinforce the concrete, even though under certain conditions they can become tamei, because anything that is attached to the ground and is not a vessel is nullified to the ground.1

In addition to the requirement that the water of the mikva be gathered in the ground, it must meet three rules (which will be explained in halakhot 7-8): a) that it not be drawn (she'uvim) in vessels; b) that its formation (its creation) not be by a person, but by the forces of nature; c) that it not come to be by means of something that is 'susceptible to tum'a'.

sections.title: The Volume of a Mikva: Forty Se'a
sections.html:
The Sages learned from the verses of the Torah that the water of the mikva must be of a quantity in which a person can immerse his entire body at once, and not limb after limb. For this it must be of the measure of one amma by one amma, to a height of three ammot, since the height of an average person, without his head, is about three ammot, and when he immerses, the water rises up and the one immersing bends slightly, and thus his head enters the water. The volume of this measure is forty se'a (Ḥagiga 11a; Tosafot Yoma 31a, s.v. 'amma'). Even a person whose body is small, who is able to immerse his body in a smaller measure than this, cannot become tahor in a mikva that does not contain forty se'a, because only a mikva that is fit to purify people in general is kosher. Even if the mikva lacks any amount at all from forty se'a, it is invalid (Ketubot 104a). Therefore, if the mikva contained exactly forty se'a, and a person immersed in it and became tahor, then since he came up from the tevila with the drops on him, the mikva no longer contains forty se'a, and it becomes invalid (SA 201:62).

In recent generations, doubt has arisen regarding the measures of the Sages, and consequently regarding the measure of forty se'a. According to the main opinion, the measure of a mikva is about 310 liters; some say at least 455 liters (Rav Ḥayim Na'eh), and some say about 650 liters (Ḥazon Ish). In practice, however, in order to avoid any doubt, and so that it will be comfortable to immerse, the custom is to prepare, lekhatḥila, mikva'ot that hold at least a thousand liters (a cubic meter). Even when one is forced to prepare a mikva of limited size, one stays as far as possible from the lowest measure, in order to keep away from the doubt.

Although the measure of the mikva was set according to the measure of an amma by an amma to a height of three ammot, there is no requirement that this be its shape. This is the rule: any mikva that contains forty se'a of water, in which the one immersing can actually immerse his entire body at once, is kosher. However, lekhatḥila one should build the mikva in a shape that is comfortable for tevila (SA 201:1; 61; Rema 201:66).

Only water is fit for a mikva, but other liquids, such as wine, oil and milk, are unfit for a mikva. Even if the mikva lacks a tiny amount (kortov) of water, it cannot be completed with wine, oil or milk (SA 201:24).2

sections.title: Between a Spring and a Mikva
sections.html:
There are two types of gatherings of water in the ground: a) a spring, whose source is groundwater, that is, water that issues from the ground; b) a pit in which rainwater collects, which is called a 'mikva'. As it is stated (Vayikra 11:36): "Only a spring or a cistern, a gathering of water, shall be pure." Spring water is fit for tevila even while it is flowing, but the water of a mikva is fit only in an 'ashboren', that is, when it stands in its place, because water is fit in the manner in which it exists in its natural state. Rainwater comes down from the sky, and as long as it is flowing its state is temporary and not fixed; only when it collects in one place does it endure, and then it can be used. In contrast, a spring always issues forth and flows, and since this is its nature and the manner of its use, it is fit for tevila even while its water is flowing (Mishna Mikva'ot 1:7-8; SA 201:2).

If another liquid, such as red wine, fell into a spring, then even though it changed the appearance of the water, since spring water is considered 'living water' (mayim ḥayim), the spring is fit for tevila. But if red wine fell into a mikva and changed the appearance of the water, then since the color of the mikva changed because of a liquid that is not water, the mikva becomes invalid. However, since the mikva already contained forty se'a of kosher water, one may add more drawn water to it until the mikva's appearance returns to the appearance of water, and it will be kosher. If the appearance of the mikva changed because the water became stale, or because vessels were rinsed in it, the mikva remains kosher (SA 201:25-28).

A spring, like a mikva, requires a measure of forty se'a for the tevila of a person; but if the spring's water is flowing, all of the spring's water, from the place where it issues until the end of its flow, is combined for the calculation of forty se'a (SA 201:1).3

sections.title: Sea and River
sections.html:
All seas, large and small, are fit for the tevila of people and of vessels. And although the water of the sea moves and sways because of the wind that creates waves, or flows because of rivers that enter it, the sea does not become invalid thereby; rather, just as a spring is fit even when its water flows by its nature, so too the sea is fit when its water flows or sways by its nature (Rashi and Tosafot, Shabbat 109a).

A river whose source is an issuing spring has the law of a spring, and it is fit for tevila even while its water is moving and flowing. In contrast, a seasonal stream (naḥal akhzav), that is, a stream that flows as a result of the rains and afterwards stops flowing, has the law of a mikva, and it is fit only when its water is collected and standing (ashboren). A river whose source is a spring, but whose water increases during the rainy season and after the snows melt, follows the majority. When most of its water is from the spring, it is fit for tevila even though its water is flowing (zoḥalim). And when most of its water is from rain or from melted snow (notfim), it has the law of a mikva, and as long as it is flowing it is unfit for tevila. However, one may immerse in such a river by surrounding the place of tevila with a partition of matting, in such a way that the flow of the river is not noticeable within the partition, and then the water within the partition will be fit for tevila (SA 201:2).4

sections.title: A Mikva Invalidated by Flowing
sections.html:
As we learned, a mikva is a gathering of water whose source is rainwater, and if its water is flowing (zoḥalim), it is disqualified from serving as a mikva. Therefore, one must take care that there be no leak from the mikva. Be-di'avad, if a crack opened in the mikva and water is flowing out of it: if, after all the water down to the height of the crack has flowed out, forty se'a will remain in the mikva, the mikva is kosher even while its water is flowing, since this flow will not cause its invalidation. But if, after all the water down to the height of the crack has flowed out, forty se'a will not remain in the mikva, then since, as a result of the flow, the mikva cannot endure, it is invalid, even though it still contains forty se'a. Only if the crack is sealed, and forty se'a remain in the mikva, will it become kosher again. When water is flowing out of a hole, one must seal it with something that is not susceptible to tum'a, such as sealing materials, or a plastic stopper, or a wooden one that has no receptacle, but not with a metal stopper or with a cloth (SA 201:50).5

Only a noticeable flow, which creates movement in the water, invalidates; but if the mikva's water flows out a little or is absorbed into the ground a little, as long as the flow is not noticeable and forty se'a remain in the mikva, the mikva is kosher (SA 201:51). Some are stringent even regarding a flow that is not noticeable (Gra). And although the main view follows the lenient opinion, lekhatḥila we take the stringent opinion into account. However, a slight drop in the water level, which is noticeable only after many hours, does not invalidate according to all opinions.6

sections.title: The Disqualification of Drawn Water
sections.html:
Drawn water (mayim she'uvim), that is, water that was detached from the ground and was in vessels, is unfit for a mikva. Even when the water was not drawn by a person but reached the vessels from the sky, for example, if a person placed vessels in his courtyard in order to catch rainwater, the rainwater caught in the vessels he placed is considered drawn and is unfit for a mikva.

Water that flows in pipes from springs and wells is not considered drawn; but if the pipe has a 'receptacle' (beit kibul), the pipe becomes a vessel, and the water that passes through it is considered drawn and is invalid. Since the water that the water company conveys through pipes often passes through receptacles, tap water reaching homes and gardens is considered drawn water (as will be explained below in halakha 12).

Not only is drawn water unfit for a mikva, but if a quantity of three log (about 900 ml) of drawn water enters rainwater that does not amount to forty se'a, all the kosher rainwater becomes invalid. Even when the three log of drawn water fell into the rainwater unintentionally, all the kosher rainwater has become invalid. And even if another forty se'a of kosher water is added to it, the mikva remains invalid. The solution is to empty the mikva of all its water and to wait for it to fill again with rainwater. But if from the outset the mikva contained rainwater in the measure of forty se'a, then even if thousands of liters of drawn water are brought into it, it will not become invalid.

Drawn water invalidates rainwater that does not amount to forty se'a provided that it fell directly into it; but if it was poured near the mikva and was drawn along the ground for a length of three tefaḥim (about 23 cm) and afterwards entered the kosher water, it was nullified to the ground and it too became kosher, provided that the rainwater constitutes the majority of the forty se'a. Therefore, if the mikva contained more than twenty se'a of rainwater, one may complete the mikva with drawn water that is poured near the mikva and is drawn along the ground into it (SA 201:44-45). This procedure is called 'hamshakha' (conveyance). The manner of hamshakha will be explained at the end of the next halakha.7

sections.title: Invalidity of Water Formed by a Person or Through Tum'a
sections.html:
Even when the mikva was not filled by means of vessels that make the water drawn, for example, if a person filled it using a pierced vessel, or if there was a rain puddle beside the mikva and a person splashed water with his hands from the puddle into the mikva, the mikva is invalid, since its formation (its creation) was done by a person and not by Heaven, that is, by the forces of nature. Even when only three log of water reached, by means of a person, a mikva that did not yet contain forty se'a, all of it becomes invalid, like the law of drawn water that fell into a deficient mikva (SA 201:15; 39).

A further condition for a pure mikva is that the water come into being in it in purity, as it is stated (Vayikra 11:36): "Only a spring or a cistern, a gathering of water, shall be pure," and the Sages expounded (Zevaḥim 25b): "Their formation shall be through purity." But if the rainwater entered the mikva by means of things that can become tamei, the water is invalid. Therefore, water that flowed into the mikva through a metal pipe that is not attached to the ground is invalid, since a metal pipe that is not attached to the ground is susceptible to tum'a. All this applies only when the water reached the mikva directly through something that is susceptible to tum'a; but if, after leaving the thing that is susceptible to tum'a, it continued to flow on the ground and then poured into the mikva, it is kosher, since in practice it entered the mikva without the aid of something that is susceptible to tum'a (SA 201:48).8

It is customary to end the conveyance of the rainwater that comes down from the roof into the mikva with a channel three tefaḥim long (about 23 cm), whose bottom is of soft concrete that can absorb water; thereby, even if an invalidity of 'drawn water', 'formed by a person' or 'formed through tum'a' befell the water, the invalidity will be remedied by this hamshakha.9

sections.title: Zeri'a and Hashaka
sections.html:
Once there is a kosher mikva, one can additionally create further mikva'ot by means of it, through 'zeri'a' (seeding) or through 'hashaka' (contact), as we shall explain:

Zeri'a: Just as a kosher mikva purifies those who immerse in it, so it purifies and renders fit drawn water that was 'sown' into it, that is, that fell or flowed into it. Even if a quantity of drawn water a thousand times greater is poured into a kosher mikva, all the water poured into it will turn into water fit for tevila. And if a great deal of water is sown into the mikva so that it overflows and fills many more pools, all the pools will be fit for tevila, since the water in them was rendered fit by zeri'a in a kosher mikva. Admittedly, there is one who holds that if no more than twenty se'a of the original rainwater remain in the mikva, the mikva becomes invalid by the words of the Sages (Ra'avad); but according to the rest of the Rishonim, a mikva can render fit through zeri'a an unlimited amount of water, and there is no need for original rainwater to remain in it, since all the water sown into it became kosher like rainwater. And so is the halakha (SA 201:15; 24).10

Hashaka: Drawn water that was put in contact with mikva water, that is, that touched the mikva water, becomes fit for tevila. That is, if there was a kosher mikva and beside it a pool of drawn water, and they are connected by a hole with a diameter of 5 cm ('kishfoferet ha-nod'), then the moment the pool's water touches the mikva water, it is rendered fit, and the pool becomes a kosher mikva. Even if the hole between the mikva and the pool is afterwards sealed, the water in the pool has already become a kosher mikva and will not become invalid again. Admittedly, there is one who holds that if the hole connecting them is sealed again, the water in the pool becomes unfit for tevila (Rabbeinu Yeruḥam). But according to halakha, once the pool's water has been in contact with the water of the otzar one time, the pool's water remains kosher forever (SA 201:52; and see Shakh 112. Nowadays, when the tevila pool is filled through hamshakha, even according to the stringent opinion the invalidity is rabbinic, as explained above in halakha 7 and note 7).

sections.title: Mikva'ot in Our Times
sections.html:
In the past, many were accustomed to immerse in springs, seas and rivers, for at a time when there was no system of pipes for supplying water, people needed to live near water sources, and consequently they used them for tevila. In places that were not near available water sources, it was customary to hew pits in the courtyard to store rainwater, and one of the pits was devoted to tevila. Following the development of solutions for transporting water and the growth of the urban population, the need arose to build mikva'ot that would serve many people. Then, if everyone immersed in the same mikva, the water would become dirty; therefore they separated the 'otzar' (reservoir) of rainwater from the tevila pool, which they would render fit by zeri'a in the otzar or by hashaka with it. In this way they could change the water in the tevila pool frequently.

In recent generations, with the rise in the standard of living, many began to be meticulous to render the water in the tevila pool fit in both ways, through zeri'a and through hashaka. That is, the mikva is rendered fit by means of two 'otzarot', each of which contains forty se'a of rainwater: a) an 'otzar zeri'a' (seeding reservoir), into which tap water is conveyed, and from which the water overflows through hamshakha into the tevila pool; b) an 'otzar hashaka' (contact reservoir), with which the tevila pool is put in contact through a hole whose diameter is at least 5 cm. At the time of tevila the hole is opened, and when no one is immersing it is closed, so that the water in the 'otzar hashaka' will not be soiled by the water in which people immersed. However, even if the hole connecting the tevila pool to the otzar hashaka was closed at the time of tevila, the tevila is valid, since opening the hole is an enhancement (hiddur) (see Igrot Moshe, YD 1:112).11

sections.title: A Mikva from Melted Ice and Snow
sections.html:
As we learned (in halakha 7), drawing invalidates water; but if the water solidified and became snow, hail or ice, it is not subject to the invalidity of drawing, for even if it is put into a vessel, since it can stand without it, it is not thereby considered drawn and does not become unfit for a mikva. Moreover, even drawn water that has already been disqualified from being used to make a mikva: if it freezes and turns into ice, the invalidity of drawn water is removed from it, and after it melts it becomes water fit for a mikva once again. Therefore, when there is a need to make a mikva in the summer, instead of waiting until the rains come to fill the otzar, one may fill it with water melted from ice.

This is how it is done: water is frozen in a freezing room and turned into blocks of ice; the blocks of ice are transported on wooden platforms that are not vessels, and the blocks of ice are placed to melt near the mikva, so that the water coming out of the ice is drawn along the ground and enters the mikva. Admittedly, some have reservations about this out of concern for various individual opinions, and therefore lekhatḥila it is preferable to make a mikva with rainwater; but when there is a need, one may prepare a mikva by bringing blocks of ice (Da'at Kohen 94; 98).12

sections.title: The Law of Water Flowing in Pipes to Homes
sections.html:
The water flowing in the system of pipes that spans the whole country generally originates in water that is fit for a mikva. In the past it came from rainwater that collected in lakes, from groundwater and from springs. Later on they began to purify sewage water, and since at the end of the purification process the water is absorbed into the ground and joins the groundwater, it becomes kosher (SA 201:47). Today, most of the water conveyed in pipes in the State of Israel is desalinated seawater, and it too is in principle fit for a mikva, since it came from the sea.

The question is whether a mikva can be made from water that flowed through the system of pipes. The law depends on the question of whether they contain a receptacle. For if the pipes have a receptacle, such as a place for collecting debris, the water flowing through them becomes invalid like drawn water (above, halakha 7; Mishna Mikva'ot 4:3; SA 201:36).

In practice, the custom is to consider the water that the water company conveys in pipes to homes and gardens as drawn water, because it often passes through a receptacle, such as the receptacle made for housing the pump or the water meter, or for separating out debris and salts. All the more so when it passes through tanks on top of water towers or beside them, or when it passes through storage tanks or water heaters on the roofs. And although the pipes with the receptacle are attached to the ground, since they had a receptacle before they were attached to the ground, even after being attached to the ground they are still considered vessels, and consequently the water passing through them is considered drawn.13

sections.title: The Renewal of Purity in Israel
sections.html:
As a result of the sin, tum'a clung to man, closing off his heart and impairing his ability to connect his thoughts, deeds and emotions to the source of his life. And since his connection to God was damaged, death clung to him. The system of mitzvot dealing with all types of tum'a and with purification from them, which is connected mainly to the Temple, is intended to raise man up from the tum'a that clung to his physical aspects and to connect him to the source of his life. Through tevila in the mikva, one who is tamei returns to the primary element of life, and thereby he can connect to God, the Source of life, ascend to the Temple, and draw life into the land and into the body, into the imagination and the emotions and all the human talents, so that they will be connected to God and will draw blessing and tikkun (repair) into the world. But for Torah study and the fulfillment of the mitzvot, which are connected to the spiritual side of man, there is no need to immerse; rather, the preparation required for them is faith and good character traits, without any need to prepare the body and the flesh for this. As the Sages said (Berakhot 22a): "Words of Torah are not susceptible to tum'a, as it is stated (Yirmiyahu 23:29): 'Is not My word like fire, says the Lord' – just as fire is not susceptible to tum'a, so too words of Torah are not susceptible to tum'a" (see Orot Ha-teḥiya 35, by our master Rav Kook).

Since the Temple was destroyed and Israel was exiled from its land, purity ceased from Israel, and only one purity remained for us, akin to the holiness of the Temple: the tevila of a woman for her purity, in order to reveal the life and holiness in the body, in the love and joy between husband and wife, which is the pinnacle of the fulfillment of the mitzva "You shall love your fellow as yourself," which is equal to all the mitzvot. For the main aim of tevila and purity is to purify actual, concrete life, with the body and the flesh, the imagination and the emotions, so that they can connect to the Source of life and grow in strength without limit.

May it be His will that through our return to our land we will merit to grow in the Torah of the Land of Israel and in its guidance for the repair of the world, and that through the purity and joy in the union of man and woman, blessing will spread to all areas of life, and we will merit the building of the Third Temple. And from the Holy of Holies the purity of the faith of Israel will be drawn forth to the whole world, in order to purify all the beliefs that are revealed in physical life with all its components. As the Sages said (Yoma 77b): "The spring that issues from the Holy of Holies at first resembles the antennae of locusts (very thin); when it reaches the entrance of the Sanctuary it becomes like a thread of the warp; when it reaches the Hall it becomes like a thread of the woof; when it reaches the entrance of the Courtyard it becomes like the mouth of a small flask." Its further flow is described in the prophecy of Yeḥezkel (47:1-12): "…and behold, water was issuing from under the threshold of the House…", and the waters of the stream will go on and increase: after they have gone a thousand ammot they will reach a person's ankles, and after another thousand ammot they will reach the knees, and after another thousand ammot they will reach the loins, and after another thousand ammot a person will no longer be able to cross them; and so they will continue to grow ever stronger: "And behold, on the bank of the stream were very many trees, on this side and on that… and they shall come into the sea, into the sea of the issuing waters (the Salt Sea, which is the Sea of Death), and the waters shall be healed. And it shall come to pass that every living creature that swarms, wherever the streams come, shall live, and there shall be a very great multitude of fish, for these waters have come there and they shall be healed, and everything shall live wherever the stream comes… And by the stream, upon its bank, on this side and on that, shall grow every tree for food, whose leaf shall not wither nor shall its fruit fail; it shall bring forth new fruit every month, because its waters issue from the Sanctuary; and its fruit shall be for food, and its leaf for healing." That is, since we will merit to be purified from tum'a and to connect to God with the full forces of life, the place where the people of Sedom sinned with the lust for money and all their other physical lusts, until it was turned into a place of death, will return to life, and its fish will multiply, and around it wondrous trees will grow, bearing fruit all year round, for every month new fruits will grow, and their leaves will be leaves of healing.

Likewise in the prophecy of Yoel (4:18): "And it shall come to pass on that day that the mountains shall drip with sweet wine, and the hills shall flow with milk, and all the streams of Yehuda shall flow with water, and a spring shall issue from the House of the Lord and shall water the Valley of Shittim." The Valley of Shittim alludes to the sin of the lust for harlotry, as it is stated (Bamidbar 25:1): "And Israel dwelt in Shittim, and the people began to commit harlotry with the daughters of Moav." And the spring that will issue from the House of the Lord will purify and repair this lust as well, which will be transformed into a longing of love between a man and his wife, and for all things of holiness, and thereby blessing will increase throughout the land.

However, the spring issuing from the Temple will purify and heal not only the Salt Sea; rather, as is alluded to in the prophecy of Yeḥezkel and stated explicitly in the prophecy of Zekharya, half of it will turn to the Mediterranean Sea, and thereby hashaka will be created between the spring issuing from the Temple, by way of the Mediterranean Sea, and the ocean that surrounds all the continents, so that through their contact with the spring issuing from the Temple, all the waters in the world will be purified and sanctified. As it is stated (Zekharya 14:8-9): "And it shall come to pass on that day that living waters shall go out from Jerusalem, half of them toward the eastern sea (the Salt Sea) and half of them toward the western sea (the Mediterranean Sea); in summer and in winter it shall be. And the Lord shall be King over all the earth; on that day the Lord shall be One and His name One."

And the tum'a of nidda will be abolished, as the Sages said: "There is no prohibition greater than that of nidda, for a woman sees blood and the Holy One, blessed be He, forbade her to her husband, but in the future to come He will permit her, as it is stated (Zekharya 13:2): …'and I will cause the spirit of impurity to pass from the land'" (Shoḥer Tov, Tehillim 146). And even the tum'a of death will pass from the world, as the Sages said: "The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: In this world you would become pure and then become impure again, but in the future to come I will purify you with an eternal purity, so that you will not become impure, as it is stated (Yeḥezkel 36:25): 'And I will sprinkle pure water upon you, and you shall be pure; from all your impurities and from all your idols I will purify you'" (Tanḥuma, Metzora 9). And death will be abolished from the world, as it is stated (Yeshayahu 11:6-9): "And the wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid… and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. And the nursing child shall play over the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the adder's den. They shall not hurt nor destroy in all My holy mountain, for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea." And it is stated (Yeshayahu 25:8): "He will swallow up death forever, and the Lord God will wipe away tears from all faces, and the reproach of His people He will remove from all the earth, for the Lord has spoken."
